job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**Scope note:** I worked only from the text you pasted (as amended October 6). I haven't seen the original bill, the redline, or the committee report, so check whether any of these points are already addressed. The statutory references below (DSHMRA, 1 U.S.C. § 109, *INS v. Chadha*) should be verified by counsel.

**Definitions (Sec. 2)**

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "by a single vessel":** Operators can split activity across several vessels, each under 10,000 tons per year, and avoid the definition. The bill has no aggregation rule for affiliates, joint ventures, or contracted vessels.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "10,000 metric tons per year":** The test is purely volume-based, so sustained pilot-scale commercial recovery below the threshold falls outside the Act. The bill also doesn't say how the threshold applies to multi-year ramp-ups or averaging.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), undefined terms:** "Seabed," "recovery," "deep seabed," and "other mineral resources" are not defined. It is unclear whether crusts, sulfides, or incidental collection during other work count, and this invites litigation over scope.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "depths greater than 200 meters":** The depth floor excludes shallow-water seabed recovery entirely. The bill also doesn't specify the reference point for measuring depth.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(B), "the Secretary":** No Secretary is designated. Sec. 6 names the Secretary of State, so readers may assume a different official was meant here.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B), "poses risks … comparable":** This catch-all has no criteria, no notice-and-comment process, and no standard of review. It gives a strong basis for arbitrary-and-capricious challenges under the APA and supports vagueness arguments.

7. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person":** The definition covers only citizens and state-law corporations. It excludes LLCs, partnerships, and trusts (LLC status under "corporation" is unclear), and it doesn't reach operators organized abroad with no U.S. entity.

8. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel":** "Equipped for" is undefined, and vessels under 5,000 gross tons fall outside the registry and reporting duties in Sec. 4 even if they exceed the tonnage threshold in Sec. 2(1)(A). The two definitions don't line up.

**Prohibition and exemptions (Sec. 3)**

9. **Sec. 3(a), "engage in":** The term is undefined. It is unclear whether it reaches financing, equipment supply, crew, processing, or sales of recovered minerals.

10. **Sec. 3(a), no import or sales ban:** Minerals recovered abroad and sold into U.S. markets are not restricted. Foreign-organized operators using foreign-flagged vessels on the high seas fall outside the prohibition, and the bill has no flag-state or port-state measures.

11. **Sec. 3(b), exploration-license grandfather:** The exemption covers "mining conducted under an exploration license" with no time limit, volume cap, or definition of exploration license. Operators could argue that commercial recovery under an exploration license is exempt indefinitely, and the bill doesn't say whether DSHMRA licenses, ISA contracts, or foreign licenses count.

12. **Sec. 3(b), "issued before the date of enactment":** The bill doesn't address renewals, amendments, transfers, or expansions after enactment. Operators could argue that a modified or transferred license was still "issued before" enactment.

13. **Sec. 3(c), environmental assessment exemption:** The exemption has no limit on volume, duration, or sampling scope, and no requirement for an approved assessment plan. It doesn't address mixed-purpose activity, so commercial tonnage could be labeled "assessment."

**Registry and reporting (Sec. 4)**

14. **Sec. 4(a), "operator":** The term is undefined, and the bill sets no registration deadline. It is unclear who must register when a vessel is chartered, sold, or reflagged.

15. **Sec. 4, no penalty:** Sec. 5(a) penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register or report carries no consequence. As written, Sec. 4 is effectively voluntary.

16. **Sec. 4(b), report content and verification:** The quarterly report must only "describe" recovery activities, with no required data such as tonnage, location, or depth. It therefore can't verify the Sec. 2(1)(A) threshold, and the bill has no public disclosure, audit, or inspection authority.

**Penalties and enforcement (Sec. 5)**

17. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8, effective-date conflict:** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the prohibition takes effect 180 days later. Either penalties apply to conduct that is still lawful, or the trigger date is ambiguous. The gap also creates a six-month window in which operators could accelerate recovery.

18. **Sec. 5(a), enforcement mechanics:** The bill names no enforcing agency and sets no penalty-assessment procedure, factors, or referral path. "Per day" is undefined for continuing violations, so it's unclear whether each vessel, each ton, or each day counts. It also has no inflation adjustment.

19. **Sec. 5(b), criminal liability:** "Willfully" is undefined, and the bill sets no standard for officer liability or for how Title 18 fines apply to entities.

20. **Sec. 5, no in rem remedies:** The bill provides no authority to seize or forfeit vessels, equipment, or minerals. Enforcement against vessels operating beyond U.S. waters depends on flag-state cooperation, which the bill doesn't require.

**International and duration provisions (Secs. 6–8)**

21. **Sec. 6, "shall seek to negotiate":** The duty ends at seeking, with no obligation to conclude an agreement and no consequence if none is reached. "Equivalent" is undefined, the bill has no reporting requirement, and it doesn't address the ISA or the UNCLOS Part XI regime. Opponents could argue the prohibition is premature or conflicts with international commitments.

22. **Sec. 7(a), removal standard:** "Serious harm" is undefined, and the NAS report has no deadline. If NAS never reports, the prohibition is effectively permanent. The joint-resolution mechanism also needs a presentment and signature analysis, and a legislative "finding" with operative effect may raise *Chadha*-type questions.

23. **Sec. 7(a) vs. Sec. 7(b), internal conflict:** Sec. 7(a) makes the prohibition last until a joint resolution is enacted, but Sec. 7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years. The bill doesn't say which controls, so the sunset could end the prohibition regardless of any NAS finding.

24. **Sec. 7(b), sunset timing and savings:** The 10-year clock runs from enactment, not from the Sec. 8 effective date, so the operative prohibition lasts about 9.5 years. There is no savings clause for violations committed before sunset, so pending penalty claims could be argued extinguished, and 1 U.S.C. § 109 may not clearly apply to a sunset.

25. **Sec. 8, grandfather timing:** The Sec. 3(b) exemption is keyed to enactment, not the effective date, so licenses issued in the 180-day gap are in a legal gray zone.

26. **Whole Act, no severability or implementation authority:** There is no severability clause, so if a court strikes the vague Sec. 2(1)(B), it's unclear whether the core Sec. 2(1)(A) prohibition survives. The bill also grants no rulemaking authority (for Sec. 2(1)(B) determinations, Sec. 4 reports, or penalty procedures) and no appropriations for NOAA or State to implement it.

**Most consequential for the markup:** items 1, 9, 11, 15, 17, and 23. These are the paths most likely to let operations continue, and the penalty and enforcement gaps (items 15–18) are the easiest for sponsors to fix as technical amendments. Your policy team should decide which of these to raise publicly and which to raise privately with committee staff.
